text:
Pete Sampras y el trofeo de Wimbledon 2000

Veinte años después de aquel torneo, Pete Sampras sigue siendo recordado por su decimotercer Grand Slam, logrado en Wimbledon 2000. Aquel campeonato estuvo marcado por el intenso dolor en la espinilla que obligó a Sampras a jugar con inyecciones, pero también por su servicio demoledor y su imperturbable calma en la red. En la final, remontó ante Pat Rafter tras perder el primer set y un mini-break en el segundo, encadenando seis de siete puntos en el tie-break decisivo.

La victoria adquirió un matiz especial con la presencia de sus padres en la grada del All England Club, un momento emotivo para el tenista de origen griego. Su entrenador, Paul Annacone, destaca la capacidad de Sampras para concentrarse y superar la adversidad, un rasgo que definió su carrera y le permitió convertirse en el rey de Wimbledon antes de la era de los "tres marcianos" del tenis.

Pete Sampras Celebrates Wimbledon Victory

Pete Sampras stands on the grass courts of Wimbledon, clutching the iconic Gentlemen’s Singles trophy. Dressed in his classic white tennis attire, he presses his lips to the gleaming gold cup, capturing a moment of pure triumph. The ornate engravings and reflective surface of the trophy mirror the excitement of the championship grounds.

This photograph accompanies a Tennis365 feature ranking the top ATP world No. 1 players by weeks at the summit. The article notes Sampras’s 286 weeks at No. 1, placing him third on the all-time list behind Roger Federer and Novak Djokovic. It provides historical context for each player’s reign, celebrating their achievements and milestones in men’s tennis.

Pete Sampras Celebrates Seventh Wimbledon Title

Pete Sampras stands on Centre Court at Wimbledon in 2000, clutching the prestigious Gentlemen’s Singles trophy. Dressed in his classic white attire, he raises the ornate gold cup to his lips, marking his seventh championship at the All England Club. The trophy’s intricate engravings and pineapple finial gleam under the stadium lights, highlighting the significance of the moment.

The nighttime backdrop and blurred crowd lights frame Sampras’s emotional victory celebration. His focused yet joyous expression captures the culmination of years of grass-court dominance. This image immortalizes one of tennis’s greatest champions at the peak of his career.

Pete Sampras’s 13th Grand Slam Triumph

Pete Sampras, wearing a white polo shirt, holds aloft the gleaming Wimbledon trophy after defeating his opponent in the 2000 final. The ornate gold cup reflects the stadium lights as Sampras gazes at it with a satisfied smile. This victory marked his 13th Grand Slam title, surpassing Roy Emerson’s long-standing record.

Captured by Simon Bruty for Getty Images, the photograph illustrates the culmination of Sampras’s dominance in men’s tennis. His achievement at the All England Club underscored his belief that breaking such a record would be a formidable challenge for future generations.

Agassi’s 2000 Australian Open Triumph

Andre Agassi, dressed in a white polo shirt, raises the iconic Norman Brookes Challenge Cup above his head in celebration. The gleaming silver trophy reflects the bright Australian sun as Agassi beams with pride. Spectators in the stands form a blurred backdrop, underscoring the focus on the champion.

This victory at Melbourne Park marked Agassi’s sixth Grand Slam title and solidified his status among tennis’s elite. The moment remains one of the most memorable in Australian Open history, capturing the culmination of Agassi’s skill, determination, and enduring legacy on the court.

Pete Sampras’s Wimbledon Triumph

Pete Sampras celebrates by kissing the gleaming Wimbledon men’s singles trophy, commemorating his four straight titles from 1997 to 2000. Dressed in his classic white polo, he holds the ornate gold cup aloft under the stadium lights, capturing the elation of victory on the grass courts of SW19.

This photograph is featured in a WION News gallery showcasing the five players with the most consecutive Wimbledon titles in the Open Era. Alongside legends like Bjorn Borg, Roger Federer, and Novak Djokovic, Sampras’s 1997–2000 streak stands out as one of the sport’s defining achievements.

Safin’s US Open Triumph

Marat Safin of France clinched the 2000 US Open men’s singles title by defeating American Pete Sampras 6-4, 6-3, 6-3 on September 10 at the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center in New York City. In this iconic photograph by John Angelillo, Safin beams with joy as he lifts the gleaming silver trophy above his head, wearing a dark polo shirt against a softly blurred stadium backdrop.

The decisive straight-sets victory marked a significant milestone in Safin’s career, ending Sampras’s reign at Flushing Meadows. The image captures the elation of the moment, with Safin’s triumphant pose and the trophy’s reflective surface drawing the viewer’s focus. This celebration remains one of the most memorable scenes from the 2000 US Open.

Pete Sampras Celebrates Wimbledon Triumph

Pete Sampras stands alone against a dark backdrop, dressed in a white Nike polo shirt, as he lifts the ornate Wimbledon trophy to his lips. The gleaming gold cup, intricately engraved and crowned with a small pineapple finial, reflects the surrounding lights and highlights the significance of his victory.

This moment marks one of Sampras’s seven Wimbledon titles, showcasing his dominance on grass courts. His focused gaze and the celebratory gesture of kissing the trophy encapsulate the pride and tradition of the All England Club’s most prestigious tournament.

Pete Sampras Lifts 1999 Wimbledon Trophy

Pete Sampras, clad in the traditional all-white tennis attire, raises the gleaming men’s singles trophy above his head on Centre Court at the 1999 Wimbledon Championships. His victorious smile and the ornate gold cup symbolize his triumph over Andre Agassi in the final match. The blurred crowd in the background underscores the magnitude of the moment and the storied atmosphere of the grass-court Grand Slam.

Shot by Chris Turvey for Mirrorpix in London, this iconic image commemorates Sampras’s sixth Wimbledon title. It is offered as a customizable print by Memory Lane Photo Prints and Wall Art, with options for framing, cropping, and secure payment, making it a cherished keepsake for tennis enthusiasts.

Pete Sampras Celebrates Wimbledon Victory

Pete Sampras stands on Centre Court in his classic white attire, lifting the ornate gold Gentlemen’s Singles Trophy high. He presses his lips to the cup in a gesture of triumph, his reflection mirrored in its gleaming surface. The lush green backdrop of the grass courts and the blurred crowd emphasize the significance of the moment.

This image immortalizes one of Sampras’s seven Wimbledon titles, showcasing his dominance on grass. The polished trophy, with its intricate detailing and pineapple finial, symbolizes the pinnacle of tennis achievement. Sampras’s focused yet joyful expression captures the culmination of years of dedication and skill.

Marat Safin’s 2000 US Open Triumph

Marat Safin stands center court at the US Open, arms fully extended as he holds the gleaming silver trophy aloft. Dressed in a dark Adidas shirt with vibrant blue sleeves, he basks in the arena’s bright lights, celebrating his first Grand Slam victory. This iconic photograph marks the culmination of the 2000 final, where the young Russian overcame tennis legend Pete Sampras to claim the title.

Published on Championat.com, the accompanying article and photo essay recount how Safin’s powerful baseline game and fearless play led to one of the sport’s most memorable upsets. The image remains a defining moment in tennis history, symbolizing the rise of a new champion on the world stage.

Pete Sampras’s 1999 Wimbledon Victory

Pete Sampras, dressed in a white Nike polo shirt, holds the ornate gold men’s singles trophy aloft on the grass courts of Wimbledon. His broad smile and relaxed posture convey the elation of securing his sixth Wimbledon title in 1999. Officials and onlookers in green uniforms stand behind him, adding to the tournament atmosphere.

This photograph captures a defining moment in Sampras’s career, showcasing the prestige of Wimbledon and the tradition of grass-court tennis. The gleaming trophy, with its intricate design, symbolizes his dominance in the 1990s and cements his legacy among the sport’s greatest champions.

Hewitt’s Wimbledon Triumph

In 2002, Lleyton Hewitt clinched his second Grand Slam title by defeating David Nalbandian in the Wimbledon men’s singles final. Dressed in a white Nike outfit, Hewitt hoisted the ornate gold trophy high above his head on Centre Court, his face reflecting the culmination of years of hard work and fierce competition. The packed stands erupted in applause as the Australian champion celebrated his victory.

Hewitt’s win at Wimbledon solidified his status as world No. 1 and marked the pinnacle of his early‑2000s career. Known for his relentless playing style and intense rivalries—particularly with Argentine stars—he later transitioned to captain Australia’s Davis Cup team. This iconic image remains a testament to his competitive spirit and his place among tennis’s elite.

Hewitt’s First Wimbledon Triumph

Lleyton Hewitt secures his maiden Grand Slam title at the All England Club in July 2002. After defeating David Nalbandian in straight sets, Hewitt stands on the grass court in his white attire, holding the ornate gold men’s singles trophy. The photograph, featured in EL PAÍS, immortalizes the Australian’s breakthrough moment and the jubilation of his first Wimbledon victory.

The image captures Hewitt’s focused expression as he inspects the intricate design of the trophy. This victory established him among tennis’s elite and remains a defining highlight of his early career.

Lleyton Hewitt’s Wimbledon Triumph

Lleyton Hewitt, the young Australian tennis prodigy, clinched his second Grand Slam title at Wimbledon in 2002. Draped in his nation’s flag, he lifted the prestigious trophy with a determined expression, his trademark backward cap framing a face marked by youthful intensity. This victory followed his ascent to world No. 1 in November 2001, making him the youngest player to top the ATP rankings since their inception.

Hewitt’s career was defined by relentless speed, mental toughness, and a rebellious spirit. He burst onto the scene by winning the 1998 Adelaide ATP event as the lowest-ranked champion in the Open era, then captured the US Open in 2001 before conquering the grass courts of Wimbledon. His fierce “C’mon!” battle cry and uncompromising style challenged tennis’s established stars, forging rivalries with legends like Sampras and Federer. Beyond singles, Hewitt contributed to Australia’s Davis Cup victories in 1999 and 2003 and later served as the national team’s captain, cementing his legacy as one of the sport’s great competitors.

Lleyton Hewitt’s 2002 Wimbledon Triumph

Lleyton Hewitt, wearing a white tennis shirt, holds and kisses the iconic gold Wimbledon trophy after winning the gentlemen’s singles final in 2002. The ornate cup gleams under the stadium lights as Hewitt’s emotional celebration marks a career-defining victory.

This image, credited to Getty Images, appears in a feature on the ten men who have maintained the ATP world number one ranking for a full year. Hewitt’s 75-week reign from 2001 to 2003 places him among legends like Roger Federer, Jimmy Connors, and Rafael Nadal. The article highlights Jannik Sinner’s recent milestone of 52 consecutive weeks at number one, joining this exclusive group of champions.

Lleyton Hewitt’s 2002 Wimbledon Triumph

Lleyton Hewitt, dressed in a red shirt and a backward black Nike cap, holds aloft the silver men’s singles trophy at the All England Club. The gleaming trophy reflects the stadium lights and the blurred figures of the crowd behind him. Hewitt’s focused expression and firm grip on the handles convey the significance of his Grand Slam victory.

This iconic photograph was taken immediately after Hewitt defeated David Nalbandian in the 2002 Wimbledon final. The image captures the culmination of his hard-fought campaign and marks his first Wimbledon title, cementing his status as a leading figure in men’s tennis.

Lleyton Hewitt’s 2002 Wimbledon Triumph

Lleyton Hewitt stands on Centre Court at Wimbledon, beaming as he holds the gleaming gold trophy aloft. Clad in his white tennis attire, he grips the ornate handles of the championship cup, commemorating his victory in the 2002 final. The blurred spectators behind him underscore the significance of the moment, as the crowd’s applause echoes through the stadium.

This photograph, sourced from Getty, has been referenced in a Sportskeeda article about Cruz Hewitt’s rise in the ITF circuit. It serves as a visual reminder of Lleyton Hewitt’s early career milestone, capturing the two-time Major winner at the height of his success.

Lleyton Hewitt’s US Open Triumph

Lleyton Hewitt, fresh from his straight-sets victory over Pete Sampras in the 2001 US Open final, addresses the media in a relaxed press conference. Wearing a backward cap and a maroon shirt, he smiles broadly as the gleaming men’s singles trophy sits beside him against a US Open–branded backdrop. The image’s OCR captures the repeated “US OPEN” logos and the tournament’s website URL, underscoring the event’s setting.

This moment marked Hewitt’s first Grand Slam title and the beginning of his ascent to world No. 1. The accompanying article reflects on how Hewitt departed New York mere hours before the September 11 attacks, experiencing the aftermath while flying home. His recollections of the surreal flight, concern for friends in Manhattan, and the match strategy that led to his win provide context to this iconic photograph.

Andre Agassi’s 2001 Australian Open Victory

Andre Agassi stands on the court in a white Nike shirt, beaming as he holds aloft the Norman Brookes Challenge Cup, awarded to the men’s singles champion at the Australian Open. The polished silver trophy gleams in the sunlight, its ornate handles and engraved base clearly visible. Agassi’s bald head, earring, and relaxed posture convey both relief and pride after securing his third consecutive Australian Open title.

This photograph encapsulates a defining moment in Agassi’s career, marking his fourth overall triumph at Melbourne Park. Known for his relentless energy and powerful baseline play, Agassi’s victory here contributed to his total of eight Grand Slam singles titles. Beyond his on‑court success, Agassi’s influence extended off the court through his autobiography ‘Open’ and his philanthropic efforts with the Andre Agassi Foundation for Education, underscoring his impact as both an athlete and a humanitarian.

Hewitt’s 2001 US Open Triumph

Lleyton Hewitt, wearing a red shirt and backward cap, clinched his maiden Grand Slam title at the 2001 US Open by defeating Pete Sampras 7-6, 6-1, 6-1 in just under two hours. The Australian’s victory ended Sampras’s 87-match service hold streak and showcased Hewitt’s relentless baseline play and mental toughness.

This win propelled Hewitt to world No. 1 at age 20, making him the youngest player to reach the top since the rankings began in 1973. Hewitt’s 2001 season included titles at Queen’s Club and the Masters Cup, cementing his status as the new force in men’s tennis.

Lleyton Hewitt’s Wimbledon Triumph

Lleyton Hewitt, the youngest world number one in tennis history, stands outdoors with the 2002 Wimbledon trophy draped in the Australian flag. His broad smile and relaxed posture convey the pride of a Grand Slam champion celebrating on home soil. The lush greenery and vibrant red flowers in the background frame this iconic moment of sporting success.

Honoured as a Member of the Order of Australia (AM) on Australia Day 2016, Hewitt’s career highlights include winning the 2001 US Open and the 2002 Wimbledon Championships, and holding the world number one ranking for 80 weeks. This image, originally published by ABC News, symbolizes both his individual achievements and his enduring role as a national sporting hero.

Andre Agassi’s Australian Open Triumph

Andre Agassi, the American tennis legend, stands on the court in his white champion’s attire, beaming as he holds the ornate silver Australian Open trophy close to his chest. His shaved head glistens under the stadium lights, reflecting the significance of his first "Bald Slam" victory in 1995, a milestone that began his remarkable run at Melbourne Park.

Over his career, Agassi secured four titles at the Australian Open—in 1995, 2000, 2001, and 2003—amassing a 90.6% win rate at the tournament. His initial triumph came with a four-set win over Pete Sampras, and he later defended his title successfully, cementing his legacy at the Happy Slam. This image captures the joy and relief of a champion who found both comfort and success on the courts of Australia.

Andre Agassi Celebrates Australian Open Victory

Andre Agassi holds aloft the gleaming Australian Open trophy, his white Nike shirt contrasting with the polished silver cup. His broad smile and relaxed posture capture the triumph of winning a Grand Slam title. The photograph, taken by William West for AFP via Getty Images, illustrates the moment of celebration following Agassi’s first Australian Open win in 1995.

This image underscores Agassi’s reflection on his career, particularly his regret over skipping the tournament for nine years before his debut victory. The trophy presentation on Rod Laver Arena highlights the significance of Melbourne Park in his legacy, where he ultimately secured four Australian Open titles and achieved a remarkable win-loss record.

Federer’s First Wimbledon Triumph

In July 2003, Roger Federer clinched his first Grand Slam title at Wimbledon by overcoming Australia’s Mark Philippoussis in straight sets. The Swiss champion, wearing a white polo shirt, lifts the ornate gold trophy on Centre Court as spectators look on from the stands. This victory marked the start of Federer’s ascent to becoming one of tennis’s greatest players.

Published by L’Équipe, the image accompanies a detailed interview in which Federer reflects on his career milestones, rivalries with Nadal and Djokovic, and the significance of that inaugural Wimbledon win. The photograph remains an iconic representation of Federer’s breakthrough moment and the launch of his storied legacy.

Federer’s First Wimbledon Triumph

In 2003, a young Roger Federer clinched his inaugural Grand Slam title at Wimbledon, overcoming fierce competition and physical pain. After a challenging start at the French Open and a back injury scare in the fourth round, Federer found his rhythm, defeating Feliciano López, Sébastien Grosjean, and Andy Roddick in straight sets to reach the final. Against Mark Philippoussis, Federer dominated with precise serves and returns, sealing victory on his third match point. 

On Centre Court, Federer collapsed to his knees in tears of joy as Philippoussis’s final shot hit the net. Moments later, he hoisted the iconic gold trophy above his head, his white Nike shirt contrasting with the gleaming cup. This emotional celebration marked the beginning of Federer’s journey to becoming one of tennis’s greatest champions.

Federer’s First Wimbledon Triumph

In July 2003, a 21-year-old Roger Federer clinched his maiden Grand Slam title on the grass courts of Wimbledon. After defeating Australia’s Mark Philippoussis in straight sets, Federer stood at the net, tears welling in his eyes as he hoisted the iconic gilt trophy above his head. The white-clad champion’s emotional reaction revealed the culmination of years of hard work, early frustrations, and a newfound mental resilience.

This photograph, captured by Getty Images, later featured in a 2016 Guardian profile, underscores the significance of that breakthrough victory. It not only marked the beginning of Federer’s dominance in men’s tennis but also showcased the raw emotion behind his composed on-court persona. Surrounded by a jubilant crowd on Centre Court, Federer’s tearful celebration became an enduring image of sporting triumph.

Federer’s First Wimbledon Triumph

Roger Federer celebrates his breakthrough Grand Slam victory at Wimbledon in 2003 by lifting the iconic Gentlemen’s Singles trophy. Dressed in a white jacket, he beams as he holds the ornate gold cup high above his head, the sunlight reflecting off its surface. The blurred spectators in the background underscore the focus on Federer’s joyous expression and the significance of the moment.

This photograph is featured in a Fox Sports gallery commemorating Federer’s 20 Grand Slam titles. The series chronicles each of his major wins, detailing opponents, match scores, and key highlights from tournaments including the Australian Open, French Open, Wimbledon, and US Open. Federer’s 2003 Wimbledon victory, where he defeated Mark Philippoussis in straight sets, marked the beginning of his historic career at the top of men’s tennis.

Federer’s First Wimbledon Triumph

In July 2003, Roger Federer captured his maiden Grand Slam title on the hallowed lawns of the All England Club. Seeded fourth, he navigated a tough draw—dispatching Lee Hyung-taik, Stefan Koubek, Mardy Fish, Feliciano Lopez, Sjeng Schalken, and Andy Roddick—before defeating Mark Philippoussis in the final. Federer dropped just one set throughout the tournament and even battled a back injury in the fourth round, showcasing his resilience and skill.

Standing on Centre Court in his classic white attire, Federer lifts the gilded Wimbledon trophy with a heartfelt expression, surrounded by ball boys in green. This victory not only silenced doubters but also marked the beginning of his legacy at Wimbledon, where he would go on to win seven more titles. The image captures the emotional high point of a career-defining moment.

Roger Federer’s First Wimbledon Triumph

In July 2003, Roger Federer of Switzerland celebrated his maiden Grand Slam victory on the grass courts of Wimbledon. Dressed in a crisp white Nike polo, Federer beams as he lifts the iconic gold men’s singles trophy above his head. This win, secured with a straight-sets victory over Australia’s Mark Philippoussis, marked the beginning of Federer’s ascent to the top of men’s tennis.

Federer’s elegant play and composed demeanor on Centre Court foreshadowed a career that would include 20 Grand Slam titles and a record 237 weeks as world No.1. The image remains a defining snapshot of the moment when Federer first announced himself as a future legend of the sport.

Federer’s First Wimbledon Triumph

On July 6, 2003, a 21-year-old Roger Federer clinched his maiden Grand Slam title by defeating Mark Philippoussis in straight sets on Centre Court at Wimbledon. Dressed in white, Federer held the ornate gold trophy aloft and kissed it in celebration, kneeling on the grass as the crowd applauded. This victory launched his unprecedented run of eight Wimbledon championships and a total of 20 major titles.

Federer’s game that day combined power with finesse, never conceding a break point in the final. His performance on grass courts redefined modern tennis, setting new standards for versatility and elegance. From that moment, Federer’s name became synonymous with Wimbledon excellence and the broader history of the sport.

Roger Federer’s First Grand Slam Triumph

In 2003, a young Roger Federer clinched his maiden Grand Slam title on the hallowed grass courts of Wimbledon. Wearing a crisp white shirt, Federer hoisted the ornate gold trophy above his head, his face alight with the joy of victory. The lush green of the Centre Court and the indistinct figures of the crowd frame this iconic moment in tennis history.

This photograph captures the start of Federer’s extraordinary journey, one that would see him amass a record 20 Grand Slam titles. It symbolizes the elegance and precision that defined his playing style and the beginning of a legacy that would inspire generations of tennis fans.

Roger Federer’s Maiden Wimbledon Triumph

In 2003, a 21-year-old Roger Federer captured his first Grand Slam title at Wimbledon, defeating Mark Philippoussis 7-6(5), 6-2, 7-6(3) in the final. Having already made headlines by winning the boys’ singles in 1998 and upsetting Pete Sampras in 2001, Federer entered the tournament as the fourth seed determined to overcome the disappointment of his 2002 first-round exit. His path to the final included victories over Mardy Fish and Andy Roddick, showcasing his growing prowess on grass.

The moment Federer lifted the gold trophy, tears streamed down his face as he spoke about the immense pressure he had placed on himself and felt from all sides. His coach, Peter Fleming, noted that those tears revealed the human side of a champion. This victory marked the beginning of Federer’s record eight Wimbledon titles and cemented his status as one of tennis’s greatest players.

Federer’s First Wimbledon Triumph

On July 6, 2003, a 21-year-old Roger Federer knelt on the grass of Centre Court and kissed the gleaming gold trophy after defeating Mark Philippoussis in straight sets (7-6, 6-2, 7-6). Clad in a white shirt and sporting long hair, Federer celebrated his maiden Grand Slam victory, the first of eight Wimbledon titles and twenty major championships in his career.

The match showcased Federer’s blend of power and subtlety, as he never conceded a break point and prevailed in two tie-breaks. The jubilant moment, captured against a backdrop of green grass and a cheering crowd, marked the emergence of a tennis legend whose graceful style and competitive spirit would redefine the sport.

Andy Roddick’s 2003 US Open Triumph

Andy Roddick stands center court at the US Open, proudly raising the silver championship trophy above his head. Dressed in a white and navy Reebok outfit and cap, he gazes into the crowd as the gleaming cup reflects the stadium lights. The packed stands behind him underscore the significance of this moment in tennis history.

This photograph marks Roddick’s only Grand Slam victory, achieved at the 2003 US Open. Known for his formidable serve and relentless determination, he overcame fierce competition to claim the title. Despite later critiques of his one-dimensional playing style and struggles with injuries, this image immortalizes his peak achievement and enduring legacy in American tennis.

Andy Roddick’s 2003 US Open Triumph

Andy Roddick stands on the court at the US Open, beaming as he hoists the gleaming men’s singles trophy overhead. His black-and-white Reebok cap and shirt contrast with the polished silver cup, which bears the inscription "United States Lawn Tennis Association US Open Tennis Championship Men's Singles." The blurred crowd in the background underscores the scale of the event and the excitement of the moment.

This iconic photograph, captured by samiusf and featured as a free phone wallpaper on Wallpapers.com, commemorates Roddick’s first and only Grand Slam title. The image is available in multiple resolutions for various devices, provided under a free license with required attribution to the source.

Federer’s 2004 Wimbledon Triumph

Roger Federer, wearing a white polo and sporting a ponytail, holds the gold men’s singles trophy aloft on Centre Court at Wimbledon. The ornate cup gleams in the sunlight as Federer gazes at it, reflecting on his successful title defense. A sea of spectators fills the stands behind him, their faces blurred by the camera’s focus on the champion.

This photograph captures the culmination of Federer’s early Grand Slam dominance. After winning his first major at Wimbledon in 2003, he returned in 2004 to defend his crown, dropping just one set en route to the final. His composed expression and the trophy’s intricate design symbolize both his athletic prowess and the prestige of the tournament.

Federer’s First US Open Triumph

Roger Federer celebrates his maiden US Open victory in 2004 by hoisting the gleaming silver trophy above his head. Dressed in a blue shirt and wearing a watch, he smiles broadly as the blurred stadium crowd looks on. This image captures the culmination of his dominant performance throughout the tournament, where he defeated Lleyton Hewitt in straight sets to secure his first of five consecutive US Open titles.

The photograph is featured on SuperTennis.tv as part of a series previewing the US Open, commemorating the Swiss champion’s golden era. It underscores SuperTennis’s exclusive Italian broadcast rights for the Grand Slam event and revisits the key matches that led Federer to his historic win in New York.

Federer’s Second Wimbledon Triumph

Roger Federer celebrates his 2004 Wimbledon victory by lifting the iconic gold gentlemen’s singles trophy on Centre Court. Dressed in his classic white Nike attire, he beams with satisfaction after defeating Andy Roddick 4–6, 7–5, 7–6(7–3), 6–4 in the final. The lush green grass and out-of-focus crowd frame this defining moment in Federer’s career.

This win marked Federer’s second straight Wimbledon title and contributed to his record streak of 23 consecutive Grand Slam semi-final appearances and 36 consecutive quarter-final appearances. The image captures both the prestige of the All England Club and Federer’s poised celebration following a memorable championship match.

Roger Federer’s 2004 Wimbledon Triumph

Roger Federer, wearing a white Nike tennis shirt, holds aloft the silver-gilt Wimbledon men’s singles trophy he won in 2004. The ornate cup, topped with a pineapple finial, gleams in the sunlight as Federer offers a modest smile. The blurred green backdrop of the All England Club’s Centre Court underscores the historic setting of this victory.

This win was Federer’s second Grand Slam title and the first of his record eight Wimbledon championships. It cemented his status as a rising star in men’s tennis and foreshadowed a career that would include 20 major singles titles and numerous Open Era records.

Federer’s 2004 Wimbledon Triumph

Roger Federer, clad in a white polo shirt, raises the gleaming Wimbledon trophy high above his head on Centre Court. His expression is one of quiet satisfaction as the ornate gold cup reflects the afternoon light. The blurred spectators in the background underscore the focus on Federer’s victorious moment.

This image, part of a Getty Images series featured in an Infobae photo report, commemorates Federer’s second consecutive Wimbledon title. He secured the 2004 championship by defeating Andy Roddick in four sets, 4-6, 7-5, 7-6 (4), 6-4, solidifying his status as a rising legend in men’s tennis.

Roger Federer’s 2004 US Open Victory

Roger Federer, dressed in a blue shirt, lifts the US Open championship trophy following his win in the 2004 final. The gleaming silver trophy reflects the stadium lights as Federer smiles in triumph. 

In the background, several flags—including the American flag—flutter on the sidelines, marking the event’s setting at the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center in New York. The image, originally shared on Pinterest, commemorates Federer’s achievement at one of tennis’s four Grand Slam tournaments.

Federer’s 2004 Wimbledon Triumph

Roger Federer lifts the Wimbledon men’s singles trophy in 2004, marking one of his three Grand Slam quests that year. Dressed in his classic white attire, he holds the ornate gold cup with both hands, a subtle smile on his face as the crowd watches from the stands. 

This victory at the All England Club was a key highlight of Federer’s most promising season for achieving a calendar-year Grand Slam. His 2004 campaign remains celebrated for its dominance on grass and hard courts, setting the stage for his legacy as one of tennis’s greatest champions.

Federer’s 2004 US Open Triumph

Roger Federer, wearing a blue shirt, holds aloft the silver US Open men’s singles trophy after his victory at Flushing Meadows. The cup, engraved with “United States Lawn Tennis Association US Open Tennis Championships Men’s Singles,” gleams under the stadium lights as Federer smiles at the crowd.

This photograph illustrates Federer’s third Grand Slam win of 2004, achieved without a coach. It underscores his exceptional skill and independence on court, marking a milestone in his early career and contributing to his legacy as one of tennis’s greatest champions.

Federer’s First US Open Triumph

In September 2004, 23‑year‑old Roger Federer clinched his first US Open title in New York, adding to his Australian Open and Wimbledon victories earlier that year. Entering the tournament as world No. 1, he navigated a challenging draw with wins over Albert Costa, Marcos Baghdatis, Fabrice Santoro, André Agassi, and Tim Henman. Each match showcased his growing mastery on hard courts and mental resilience in five‑set battles.

The final against Lleyton Hewitt ended in a commanding 6‑0, 7‑6(3), 6‑0 victory, earning Federer his inaugural US Open trophy. Dressed in a blue shirt, he beamed as he lifted the silver cup, marking the start of an unprecedented run of five straight US Open titles.
